prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 as an incretin hormone, of its active form and of its physiological actions, which opened the way to incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement prize for B031 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After round 1 I have retested it on what a discovery prize is meant to reward, a specific finding that changed a field, and not on the fact that all six of us arrived at the same trio from independent openings. The unbroken chain is proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, the human physiology of secretion and insulinotropic action, receptor biology, and then durable receptor agonism with glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit confirmed in large independent trials. That reasoning does not depend on the support count. The recognition is not premature, and the discovery side lies inside the three credited names. The citation is worded to name the physiology and the active peptide and also the therapies that followed, as Wahren-Herlenius asked, so that leaving out Knudsen does not read as a verdict that the drugs were unimportant.
statement.case_against: The attribution weakness is real and round 1 did not remove it. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide relative to the Habener group is unsettled, and we are all relying on recollection of that record, not on anything in the supplied evidence. Knudsen's long-acting analogue design is what turned the biology into a medicine, so the physiology trio can be criticised for crediting the earlier half of the story. The three-person cap also means no second part is possible without cutting the GLP-1 trio, so any second achievement would be bought at the cost of a core discoverer. Long-term safety, durability of weight loss and the newer indications are still being characterised, and the citation should not overclaim them.

responses.point: Moved from B046 first and a Knudsen-for-Mojsov trio to the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio, and asked that the citation also name the therapies that followed and that Mojsov's priority claim be scrutinised, not assumed.
responses.response: I accept both requests. The citation now names the therapies enabled by the discovery, so the omission of Knudsen is not presented as a judgment on drug development. On priority, I agree it cannot be called settled, and I will not treat it as settled. What I can say from the supplied evidence is that Mojsov's work on the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is documented and is the reason I include her. The Habener group's claim is the one live risk to the name list. If it were shown to outweigh hers, the committee would have to rethink the third slot, and in that case Knudsen would be the natural candidate. Without that showing, I see no reason to drop the identification of the active peptide in favour of the downstream engineering. I also thank you for the candour in saying your view changed after the openings. I weigh B046 as a mature, clean candidate, but I keep it behind B031 on breadth and on the originality problem I raised in round 1.

responses.point: As chair and as someone who wrote the citation around discovery of the hormone and its actions, asked whether leaving Knudsen out remains defensible at the final ballot, and noted that the deciding argument between Mojsov and Knudsen is discovery of the active peptide versus development of long-acting analogues.
responses.response: I think it is defensible, and I would state the principle openly in the record. A discovery prize with a three-name cap should centre on the identification and physiology of the hormone, because the later pharmacology depended on that step and not the reverse. Knudsen's acylated analogues are outstanding, but they are a development programme inside a company, which makes individual credit harder to separate. That is a judgment about this cap and this achievement, not about the importance of the drugs, and the citation language is meant to carry that. I also hold to my round-1 view that optogenetics is a discovery about a light-gated channel and not only a tool. Even so, we agree the six-name credit is the decisive problem, and your question about whether that makes it unsuitable this year regardless of merit is one I answer yes for 2026: I cannot find a principled trio, and I am not prepared to invent one.

responses.point: Argued that a second part such as CAR-T would improve fairness only if the Eshhar gap could be settled, that pairing it with GLP-1 just for a combined clinical headline would dilute a strong single prize, and that imatinib is late and already recognised by Lasker awards.
responses.response: I agree on both counts. A two-part prize would force one of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov out to stay within three names, which trades a defensible core for a headline. In round 1 I said that if a second part were wanted I would choose CAR-T. Reading your argument and Svenningsson-Per's doubt about Rosenberg's link to CAR-specific engineering, I now think even that is too weak. A June, Sadelain and Rosenberg trio would implicitly settle credit for the first chimeric receptor concept without naming Eshhar, and I will not support it as a second part unless that record is resolved. I therefore keep CAR-T as an alternative only. I also accept your point on imatinib: my earlier hesitation about BCR-ABL discovery credit and the Lasker recognition stands, and it is why B012 is not among my alternatives.

responses.point: Treats the unfolded protein response (Mori and Walter) as conceptually original, mature and cleanly attributed, a sound second part of a two-achievement prize, and asked by implication whether its disease relevance justifies waiting.
responses.response: I take the originality and maturity of B042 seriously and I agree the two-name credit is tidy. The chair asked whether anyone sees a concrete clinical anchor that would move it ahead. I do not. Its therapeutic translation in diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer is still partial, and the mammalian PERK and ATF6 branches, with Ron and Kaufman, lie outside the credit, so the prize would reward a yeast-derived framework that others extended. As a basic-science prize it is defensible and likely to be strong in a later year. I do not support it as the second part now, because adding it would still require cutting the GLP-1 trio, and I would not make that cut to pair a basic-science discovery with a clinical one.

responses.point: Holds optogenetics as the first alternative because the channelrhodopsin work is a genuine discovery with exceptional breadth, while accepting that its medical impact is still emerging and that six names cannot fit into three.
responses.response: We are close here. I rank optogenetics as my first alternative for the same reasons, and the fairness cost is the main reason it is not first. Following your point and Wahren-Herlenius's, I would weight demonstrated effect on human disease more heavily than methodological breadth for a Physiology or Medicine prize, and clinical use of optogenetics is only beginning. Any trio of Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel omits Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and Linnarsson's variant with Miesenböck shows that members cannot agree on the principle for choosing. Until the committee can defend that principle, I would keep it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide survives comparison with the Habener group's claim. I cannot verify this from the supplied evidence and it is the one issue that could change the name list.
Whether the committee will accept that the three-name cap should favour discovery and physiology over analogue development, which is a judgment about this achievement, not about Knudsen's importance.
How the citation should describe long-term safety, durability of weight loss and newer indications without overclaiming.
Whether, for the alternatives, credit can be defended: Eshhar for CAR-T and Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck for optogenetics.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate. My documented work on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not involve the credited names. I note the previously disclosed co-authorships with Svenningsson (about twenty works) and El-Manira (one, in 2009), which concern subjects unrelated to the shortlist, and the earlier Salk-period collaboration with Ronald Evans on nuclear receptors, who is not a credited name. I infer no ties from shared institutions or topics and claim no confidential committee information.
